Affordable replacement for OEM fridge filters - I wanted to post a review on these filters to clear some things up. One of the leading negative reviews points out that the openings are different shapes from the original. This is true, but if the reviewer had taken a moment to look into their filter housing they would realize that this hole shape does not matter. This is simply an opening for water to flow. Water doesn't care if it is a square or round hole it is passing through. If you look at the housing you will see that the filter seals to the housing where the two O-rings are. The inner hole could be a triangle for all it matters. The inner hole has no way of creating a leak.

With that said. The filter has worked well for the past month of so that I have had it installed. A cheap alternative to OEM filters. We've all seen how cheap brand name filters can be from refillable pitchers. This is essentially the same thing but sealed, there is no reason a "cheap" filter should be too hard to believe.

If you pick the right seller, you can get a real OEM. - If your LG washing machine starts making strange sounds like grinding during the drain cycles, DON'T WAIT. Get a new pump today and keep it because the washer is soon (within two weeks in our case) going to poop out and give you the "OE" code. When that happens, you'll have the pump on hand instead of having to wait days for it to arrive.

Be careful of the seller or you run the risk of getting a non OEM part. While the price varies, I paid about $9 more and picked Amazon itself as the seller versus any of the other "fulfilled by Amazon" orders which are a grab bag of vendors. Mine appears to be a true LG OEM part.

The best repair guide can be found on YouTube under the title "Washing Machine Repair - Replacing the Drain Pump (LG Part # 4681EA2001T)." That's the video I followed and it took about an hour total. The hardest part is replacing the rubber drain collar around the door. Once you get that, it's game on.

A few tips:
Save all the screws and put them back into the same hole you removed them from. For instance, when you take the front off, put the loose screw back a just a few turns into its hole. There's about a dozen screws, all different, and all hard to tell apart once they're jumbled up.

Make sure you clean all the parts you've removed. The washer gets a lot of scale, funk, fumunda cheese, etc. in all the internals. It's nasty. That soap tray...hot mess to clean it out especially in the far back.

Got it done, but had to work outside the lines. - I am giving this kit a 3 star. The blue wheel bearings were an exact match. The new belt was an exact fit. This is where it got frustrating. The white tensioning wheel was chipped on the edge which would have caused the belt to catch and jump off. So I had to improvise. I opted to use the old tension arm. Then I learned the shoulder of the pin was slightly different diameter than the original, so I had to shim the new arm pin. I had to press out the bearings from the broken wheel only to realize they were slightly bigger than the original wheel bushing. I had to carefully press out the original bushing without damaging the wheel. I then had to sand the opening larger to accommodate the new bearings. Finally, I pressed the new bearings into the old wheel, and installed the old wheel onto the new arm. The good news. The replacement sealed bearings will likely be 100x better than the original brass bushing. I am pretty handy in most cases and enjoy having to work outside of the lines. Most people would not enjoy this process. If the wheel hadn't been broken, I am sure it would have worked great. It came in a thin plastic bag from Amazon, and likely was damaged in transport. The replacement components themselves are probably very solid if they come intact.

Make sure to troubleshoot and replace all parts while you have the dryer opened up - My 20 year old dryer decided that it was going to heat at it's hottest setting to the point of scalding my hands when removing the clothes from the dryer and causing a major case of wrinkles in my work Polo's. After going to YouTube to find out how to diagnose the issue, I found that there are a few things to check. First thing you will need to do is open the back of the dryer, with it unplugged, and check the Thermal Fuse. This can be done with a multi-meter or temporarily jump the two connectors/blade terminals and check if the Dryer runs at the correct temp for all cycles. Since I had the dryer taken apart I figured I would clean out the blower fan area and the fan ducting as well as the entire "innards" of the dryer. After temporarily jumping the thermal fuse I found that it had kicked the bucket as the dryer started to work again due to jumping out the fuse. Did I say that this dryer is 20 years old and the original fuse lasted that long? So I decided that since I have the thing open I might as well replace the other 20 Year old electrical components that were back there. These Items included: the Thermal Fuse, Cycling Thermostat, High Limit Dryer Thermostat and Dryer Thermal cut off. Each have their own job and purpose, so don't skimp out and think you can get away with changing the item that has failed, because if that item failed the others will follow. Did I mention my Dryer is 20 years old? As A side note; I also checked the Heating Element and found that one of the coils had warped and contacted/welded itself the the element body, this is what took out the fuse. A pair of needle nose pliers and a steady hand detached the coil and re-positioned the coil in its original shape and placement. My 20 year old dryer, that was a wedding gift to my wife when she married her fist husband now works like a champ!

One thing I've learned with these stainless steel filters is that you cannot use finely ground coffee in them or they get gunked up and no longer work. As with any pour-over (except for Oxo's, which takes care of it for you), you pour a little, wait about 30 seconds for the grounds to bloom, then finish the pour by spiraling out from the center. But because the water is dripping through fairly quickly, how do you know when you've poured too much?

I'll figure it out.

I have a Kenmore Elite hood and wasn't sure if these would work, but since the photos of the hood appeared very similar to mine, I figured I'd try them since both sides of the center one was broken 11 years ago when I moved in, and now another side broke. I'm not a duct tape person and my screens need to be in place.

My old brackets are plastic (these are spring metal with a hole in the center!) so I carefully bent and broke off the remaining bracket and a half. I left the 3 rivets intact, cleaned the areas with alcohol where the new ones would adhere, dried them and cleaned and dried them again. I took a pair of scissors and poked a hole in the adhesive where the hole is on each, peeled off the protective paper, pressed the brackets over the rivets, and inserted the screens! Done deal!

Oh, the frames have 2 notches cut out that, if you feel the front of the hood where those match to, would be to hold the screens in place. After many years, those notches were bent inward. I took something metel and, placing it gently inside the holes, bent the frame back to flatten them out.

Just like new, no more falling out when I close a cabinet! Being metal, I'm sure I'll never have to replace them EVER!
